newsitem.title: USA: Peru may have already bought back debt-US analysts.
newsitem.headline: Peru may have already bought back debt-US analysts.

text.p: Peru, which announced a plan on Friday to repurchase some of its foreign commercial debt, may have already bought back the paper, according to Wall Street analysts.

The Peruvian government said Friday that it had told bank creditors of its intention to buy back $1.265 billion of principal and $1.217 billion of past-due interest at the upcoming closing of its Brady debt restructuring accord.
But U.S. analysts said the statement was more a signal of how much debt Peru has already bought back than an indication of future activity.
"They had already bought that back," said the chief Brady bond trader at one U.S. investment bank. "That was just their way of announcing to the world how much they bought back."

The government said last week that, once the Brady restructuring is concluded, the foreign debt would be reduced to a nominal value of $4.6 billion, of which $3.8 billion would be past-due interest, from an original $10.657 billion.

But rumors of Peru buying back debt have circulated in the market for around a year. In the past few months, emerging market traders have speculated that the high prices of Peruvian debt were linked to decreased supply due to buybacks.
The government reportedly asked two foreign banks to acquire the paper, market sources said.

"My understanding was that they did the buyback and some firms were holding it for them," said a quantitative analyst at another U.S. investment bank. "Now they were just able to formally get it back from them."

"If you look at the terms of the Brady restructuring, one option for people was to tender in a buyback," one Brady trader said. "That's how Peru was going to get out of their bonds that they bought covertly."
On a May visit to New York, Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori had told Reuters that the government intended to make the repurchases in August.
The size of the outlined buybacks was in line with market perceptions, analysts said.
